'''Philippa Garrett Fawcett''' (4 April 1868 – 10 June 1948) was an English mathematician and educator. She was the first woman to obtain the top score in the Cambridge [[Mathematical Tripos]] exams. She taught at [[Newnham College, Cambridge]], and at the normal school (teacher training college) in [[Johannesburg]], and she became an administrator for the [[London County Council]].

==Family==
Philippa Garrett Fawcett was born on 4 April 1868,<ref>{{cite ODNB |id=39169 |title=Fawcett, Philippa Garrett}}</ref> the daughter of the [[suffragist]] [[Millicent Fawcett]] (née Garrett) and [[Henry Fawcett]] [[Member of Parliament|MP]], Professor of [[Political Economy]] at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]] and [[United Kingdom Postmaster General|Postmaster General]] in [[William Ewart Gladstone|Gladstone's]] [[Premierships of William Ewart Gladstone#Second government (1880–1885)|second government]].<ref name="Hansard Vol. 293: Thurs 6 Nov 1884">{{cite web | title=Death Of The Right Hon Henry Fawcett, Postmaster General | website=Hansard | url=https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/1884-11-06/debates/fd36fcd4-335a-4bd4-ad7c-d775e8ad70c2/DeathOfTheRightHonHenryFawcettPostmasterGeneral | access-date=27 October 2023}}</ref> Her aunt was [[Elizabeth Garrett Anderson]], the first English female doctor. When her father died, she and her mother went to live with Millicent's sister [[Agnes Garrett]], who had set up an interior design business on [[Gower Street, London|Gower Street]], [[Bloomsbury]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Crawford |first=Elizabeth |author-link=Elizabeth Crawford (historian) |title=Spirited Women of Gower Street: The Garretts and their Circle |url=https://www.ucl.ac.uk/bloomsbury-project/articles/events/conference2011/crawford.pdf |accessdate=12 July 2018 |work=Bloomsbury Project |publisher=[[University College London]] |archive-date=27 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160527211934/http://www.ucl.ac.uk/bloomsbury-project/articles/events/conference2011/crawford.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Education==
Philippa Fawcett was educated at [[Bedford College, London]]<ref name="Yale University Press">{{Cite book|title=Victorian Bloomsbury by Rosemary Ashton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u9gDEx6iZ5EC&q=a+second+generation+of+feminists+attended+Bedford+College+after+its+removal+from+bloomsbury&pg=PA235|accessdate=11 June 2018|isbn=9780300154474|last1=Ashton|first1=Rosemary|date=13 November 2012| publisher=Yale University Press }}</ref> (now [[Royal Holloway]]), and [[Newnham College, Cambridge]], which had been co-founded by her mother.

In 1890, Fawcett became the first woman to obtain the top score in the Cambridge Mathematical Tripos exam,<ref name="agnesscott">{{cite web|url=http://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/fawcett.htm|title=Philippa Garrett Fawcett|website=Agnesscott.edu|access-date=25 January 2014}}</ref><ref name="smithsonianmag">{{cite web|url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-woman-who-bested-the-men-at-math-120480965/|title=The Woman Who Bested the Men at Math &#124; History &#124; Smithsonian|website=Smithsonianmag.com|access-date=25 January 2014}}</ref> but since she could not receive a degree from Cambridge due to being a woman, she could not be the [[senior wrangler]].<ref name="auto1Hill">Hill, Leslie. ''Sex, Suffrage and the Stage: First Wave Feminism in British Theatre''. United Kingdom: Bloomsbury Publishing, 2018.</ref><ref name="Tideauto">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/the-rising-tide|title=The Rising Tide: Women at Cambridge|first=Stuart|last=Roberts|date=14 October 2019|website=www.cam.ac.uk}}</ref> Cambridge did not offer degrees to women until 1948.<ref name="Tideauto"/> No woman became the senior wrangler until [[Ruth Hendry]] in 1992.<ref name="Queens' College - The Bridge - Issue 4 - Spring 2016">{{cite web | title=Queens' College | website=Issuu | date=29 March 2016 | url=https://issuu.com/ciconiltd/docs/queens_bridge_spring_2016 | access-date=27 October 2023 | archive-date=27 October 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231027001926/https://issuu.com/ciconiltd/docs/queens_bridge_spring_2016 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

An anonymous poem written in 1890 paying tribute to Fawcett's Tripos achievement climaxes with the following two stanzas, mentioning the other respected mathematicians [[Arthur Cayley]] and [[George Salmon]]:<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/fawcett.htm|title=Philippa Garrett Fawcett|website=www.agnesscott.edu|access-date=29 June 2019}}</ref><blockquote><poem>
Curve and angle let her con and
Parallelopipedon and
Parallelogram
    Few can equal, none can beat her
    At eliminating theta
By the river Cam.

May she increase in knowledge daily
Till the great Professor Cayley
Owns himself surpassed
    Till the great Professor Salmon
    Votes his own achievements gammon
And admires aghast.
</poem></blockquote>Coming amidst the [[women's suffrage]] movement, Fawcett's feat gathered worldwide media coverage, spurring much discussion about women's capacities and rights. The lead story in the ''[[The Daily Telegraph|Telegraph]]'' the following day said:
{{centered pull quote| Once again has woman demonstrated her superiority in the face of an incredulous and somewhat unsympathetic world&nbsp;... And now the last trench has been carried by Amazonian assault, and the whole citadel of learning lies open and defenceless before the victorious students of Newnham and Girton. There is no longer any field of learning in which the lady student does not excel.<ref>Series, Caroline. "And what became of the women?", ''Mathematical Spectrum'', Vol. 30 (1997/8), 49–52</ref>}}

==Career==
[[File:Philippa Fawcett in her room at Newnham College.jpg|left|thumb|Fawcett in her room at Newnham College (1891)]]
Following Fawcett's achievement in the Tripos, she won the [[Marion Kennedy]] scholarship at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]]<ref name=newn>[http://www.newn.cam.ac.uk/about/history/biographies/ Marion Kennedy], Newnham College, Retrieved 22 June 2017</ref> through which she conducted research in [[fluid dynamics]]. Her published papers include "Note on the Motion of Solids in a Liquid".<ref>{{cite journal
|last       = Fawcett
|first      = Philippa
|date       = 1893
|title      = Note on the Motion of Solids in a Liquid
|url        = http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?PPN600494829_0026/DMDLOG_0035
|journal    = Quarterly Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics
|volume     = 26
|pages      = 231–258
|access-date = 4 May 2018
}}</ref>
She was appointed a college lecturer in mathematics at Newnham College, a position she held for 10 years.<ref>[http://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/fawcett.htm "Philippa Fawcett", Biographies of Women Mathematicians], [[Agnes Scott College]]</ref> In this capacity, her teaching abilities received considerable praise. One student wrote:

{{centered pull quote| What I remember most vividly of Miss Fawcett's coaching was her concentration, speed, and infectious delight in what she was teaching. She was ruthless towards mistakes and carelessness&nbsp;... My deepest debt to her is a sense of the unity of all truth, from the smallest detail to the highest that we know<ref>Newnham College Roll Letter, February 1949, 46–54. Newnham College Archives.</ref> }}

Fawcett left Cambridge in 1902, when she was appointed as a lecturer to train mathematics teachers at the [[normal school|Normal School]] (teacher training college) in [[Johannesburg]], then in [[Transvaal Colony]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.slonfawcett.org.uk/userfiles/documents/2012%20philippa%20fawcett%20biography.pdf |title=South London Fawcett Group Biography |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140311193735/http://www.slonfawcett.org.uk/userfiles/documents/2012%20philippa%20fawcett%20biography.pdf |archive-date=11 March 2014 |url-status=usurped}}</ref> now [[University of Pretoria#Groenkloof, Pretoria|part of the University of Pretoria]], South Africa. She remained there, setting up schools throughout the country, until 1905, when she returned to Britain to take a position in the administration of education for [[London County Council]]. At the LCC, in her work developing [[secondary school]]s, she attained a high rank. Denied a Cambridge degree by reason of her sex, she was one of the [[steamboat ladies]] who travelled to Ireland between 1904 and 1907 to receive an [[ad eundem degree|''ad eundem'']] University of Dublin degree at [[Trinity College Dublin|Trinity College]].<ref name="steamboat">{{cite ODNB |url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/theme/61643 |title=Steamboat ladies (''act.'' 1904–1907) |last1=Parkes |first1=Susan M. |year=2004 |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/61643 }}</ref>

Fawcett maintained strong links with Newnham College throughout her life. The Fawcett building (1938) was named in recognition of her contribution to the college, and that of her family. She died in [[Hendon]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.freebmd.org.uk/cgi/information.pl?cite=%2B8yrgqJrhMq%2BSndcCmkUjQ&scan=1|title=Index entry|accessdate=17 April 2023|work=FreeBMD|publisher=ONS}}</ref> on 10 June 1948, two months after her 80th birthday, a month after the Grace that allowed women to be awarded the Cambridge BA degree received royal assent (see [[University of Cambridge#Women's education|women's education at the University of Cambridge]]).<ref>[[Stephen Siklos]], official [[Newnham College|Newnham]] biography of [http://www.newn.cam.ac.uk/about-newnham/college-history/biographies/content/philippa-fawcett/  Philippa Fawcett] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160116163850/http://www.newn.cam.ac.uk/about-newnham/college-history/biographies/content/philippa-fawcett |date=16 January 2016 }}, 2004.</ref>

== Legacy ==
The Philippa Fawcett Internship Programme is a summer research program at the [[Centre for Mathematical Sciences (Cambridge)|Centre for Mathematical Sciences]] in the [[University of Cambridge]]. It received its first group of interns in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/internships/philippa-fawcett/philippa-fawcett-internship-programme|title=Philippa Fawcett Internship Programme &#124; Philippa Fawcett Internship Programme|website=www.maths.cam.ac.uk|access-date=26 April 2022|archive-date=1 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220701102203/https://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/internships/philippa-fawcett/philippa-fawcett-internship-programme|url-status=dead}}</ref>

On the [[University of Cambridge]]'s [[West Cambridge]] site, Philippa Fawcett Drive sits alongside roads named after other celebrated contributors to [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM subjects]], such as [[Ada Lovelace]], [[Charles Babbage]], and [[J. J. Thomson]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://map.cam.ac.uk/West+Cambridge+Site#52.210707,0.089934,15|title=West Cambridge Site: Map of the University of Cambridge|website=map.cam.ac.uk|access-date=29 June 2019|archive-date=1 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201101122249/https://map.cam.ac.uk/West+Cambridge+Site#52.210707,0.089934,15|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The [[Philippa Fawcett Teaching College]] was named after her.<ref>{{cite web |title=Philippa Fawcett Training College for Teachers, 1954 |url=https://www.layersoflondon.org/map/records/philippa-fawcett-training-college-for-teachers-1954 |website=www.layersoflondon.org |access-date=7 October 2023}}</ref>
